CausalChain: DDR gene mutations → Accumulation of DNA damage → Increased TMB and neoantigen load → Activation of TGF-β signaling → Upregulation of PD-L1 expression and recruitment of immunosuppressive cells → Establishment of an immune 'cold' tumor microenvironment → Reduced efficacy of ICIs
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancers with DDR gene alterations, TGF-β signaling is activated as a compensatory response to high TMB, leading to enhanced PD-L1 expression and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Combined inhibition of TGF-β and PD-L1 will overcome this immune resistance and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in this molecular subset of BTC.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) often harbor DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations that contribute to a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and potential neoantigen generation. Paradoxically, many of these tumors remain unresponsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), suggesting the involvement of additional immunosuppressive mechanisms. We propose that DDR deficiencies in BTC lead to compensatory activation of TGF-β signaling, which in turn upregulates PD-L1 expression and recruits immune suppressor cells, such as tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs). This sequence of events could create an immune 'cold' microenvironment despite a high neoantigen load. Thus, BTC patients with DDR alterations may benefit more from combination therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block PD-L1 and TGF-β signaling to overcome immune resistance.
